units: two neighbouring workshops work on opposing principles
the joiner takes material away with his cutting tool
the wood comes off as a curled ribbon
the smith reshapes hot metal without losing any of it
the bar changes shape under the blows
both craftsmen show patience of the same kind
every material warns the maker where it will resist
ignoring that warning leads to breaking the piece
text: Walk into two workshops that stand side by side and the rules seem to reverse. In the first, the joiner leans on his plane and the timber gives way under the blade; what comes off curls into a long ribbon and drops at his feet. Stroke by stroke he takes substance away, until the board runs smooth beneath the palm. In the second nothing leaves at all. The smith brings his hammer down on hot metal and the bar stretches, thickens and bends, yet not a grain of it is lost. One subtracts, the other pushes shape about. Even so, the patience is of one kind: both men listen to what they hold, sensing where it will fight and where it will yield. Timber speaks through its grain, iron through its colour. Miss that warning and the piece breaks, and the room around you goes awkwardly quiet.

units: a beginner recounts his first months in the locksmith trade
the clamping tool holds the piece without marking it
the teeth of the shaping tool clog when it is used askew
the head of the workshop makes a sheet-metal checking template
a screw tightened too far snapped off in its hole
polishing before truing means starting again
the upkeep habits include greasing the jaws
classroom theory seemed useless to him before hands-on work
text: An apprentice sets out his first half-year in the locksmith's workshop as three strings of memories. Tools to begin with: the vice that grips a piece without leaving a mark, the file whose teeth clog the moment you come at the work sideways, the sheet-metal template the foreman cuts so that every angle can be checked. Then the mistakes: a notch driven too deep, a screw forced until it snapped off in its hole, a face polished before it had been trued, which meant starting the whole thing over. Then the habits: clearing the teeth with copper wire, oiling the jaws, sorting templates by profile. Everything learnt in the classroom, he says, was worth nothing to him until he had felt the metal push back against the file. The right movement is learnt by the hand as much as by the head.

units: the workpiece must be held fast before anything begins
the marks are scored with a metal point
the cavity is roughed out first with a chisel in short cuts
the bottom of the cavity is finished with a hollow tool
a fit that is too slack weakens the joint
the male part is sawn on the outside of the line
a dry trial checks that entry takes moderate pressure
gluing happens only once that trial has gone well
text: Before a mortise and tenon joint goes together, wipe the bench clear and make sure the workpiece cannot shift a hair under the hand. Marking comes first: score both parts with a steel point, holding the gauge flat against the edge so the lines stay true. Rough out the mortise with a chisel, taking short cuts and working outwards from the middle. Finish the bottom with a gouge and leave the cheeks alone, because a slack fit will ruin the strength of the whole thing. Only then saw the tenon, keeping the blade outside the line, and bring it down to size with fine paring, a shaving at a time. Bring the two parts together dry: if they close under steady pressure from the palm, the fit is right. Glue goes on after that trial and not before, and the joint is drawn up in a press.

units: the last tannery in the valley is to stop trading
the price of power has risen steeply
the vats of the works are worn out
the expected buyer dropped the plan for want of money
the leather workshops nearby will have to buy from far off
waiting times for supplies will grow longer
the works that is closing took two trainees a year
a takeover run as a cooperative is being talked of locally
text: The last tannery in the valley is to shut its doors, and the leather workshops around it are uneasy. The chain that led here is easy enough to follow: the price of power climbed steeply, the vats were worn past repair, and the buyer everyone expected walked away for want of ready money. The consequence is already plain next door. Workshops that bought their hides a few steps from their own gate must now order them from far off, with longer waits and quality that is much harder to judge. A less obvious loss falls on training: the tannery took two trainees each year, and it was the only place nearby where vegetable tanning could be learnt. Those who run the valley speak of a takeover held as a cooperative. The makers fear the order books will empty long before anything of the sort arrives.

units: wood dust takes over the whole workshop
it works its way into the joints of the machines
it sets the man at the saw coughing
opening the windows only moves the cloud about
each machine has been joined to a flexible hose
an extraction box has been set up outdoors
a cloth filter holds back the finest particles
the waste that is collected beds a neighbour's animals
text: Push the door of that workshop open and the trouble announces itself: sawdust. It lies over the floor, clings to the beams, works into the hinges of every machine and sets the man at the saw coughing before the week is out. The windows stay open, yet the draught only walks the cloud from one end of the room to the other. What the joiner came up with is nothing clever. Each machine now feeds a flexible hose running to an extraction box that sits outdoors under a sheet of roofing. A cloth filter holds back the finest of it, and a sack catches the rest. He still sweeps, of course, but he no longer breathes his own trade. The dust, rather than going on the fire, goes to a neighbour who beds his animals on it. The air in there, he swears, smells of cut wood once more, and not of grey powder.

units: the writer weighs learning at a screen against learning at the bench
film lets a movement be stopped and taken apart
teaching in a room wastes no material
the workshop is costly and wears the machines
every attempt that fails throws timber away
only the workshop passes on the feel of the tool
a tired arm warns of pressure wrongly applied
the writer holds that the saving made in the room will be paid for later
text: Should a manual trade be learnt in front of a screen or in front of a bench? Training centres are split on it, and the comparison deserves to be made without flattery. The teaching room has a real advantage: a movement can be watched on film, stopped, taken apart, a posture corrected without spoiling a single board. The workshop, by contrast, is expensive, it wears the machines out, and every attempt that fails costs timber. Yet it gives what no screen will ever pass on: the tool trembling in the palm, the smell of a glue that is not taking, the ache in the forearm that warns of a bad line of pressure. Training that drops all of this turns out people who can explain a joint without being able to hold one. The sums are wrong, then: what the room saves, the bench pays for later.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: those in the village name her by her trade alone
her hands carry old scars
she no longer explains where those wounds came from
her tools are ranked by width on her bench
the handle of her mallet has been worn smooth by use
a grinding wheel is used to bring the edges back
she holds that a block is chosen before it is shaped
she refuses to show work that is unfinished
about ten pupils have passed through her workshop
she started as a labourer before she touched a carving tool
text: In the village she is known as the stone carver, and the title is enough for her. Her hands first: broad, dry, crossed with old cuts whose stories she no longer bothers to tell. Then the tools, laid out on the bench with something close to tenderness, the mallet with its handle worn smooth, the chisels ranked by width, the grinding wheel that brings back an edge and fills the place with a clear hiss. Then her early years: she came in as a labourer and pushed a barrow for a whole year before anyone put a chisel in her hand. Then what she holds to: a block is chosen before it is cut, a flaw is worked round rather than hidden, and unfinished work is shown to nobody at all. She has trained ten or so pupils, and three of them still carve in the valley. They will cut truly, she says, on the day they stop counting their blows.

units: a panel judges a chest by following the order of its making
the timber chosen holds an even colour
the joint marks were not taken from one single template
a gap shows at the corner set at the back
the cuts made are clean and closely fitted
the finishing stage lets the judges down
abrasive marks remain beside the metal fittings
the wax went on to a surface still carrying dust
the piece is called sound in spite of a rushed last stage
text: The chest put before the panel is best judged in the order it was built. The choice of timber comes first, and it could hardly be bettered: cut on the quarter, quiet grain, a colour that holds steady from one board to the next. The setting out already wavers, since the dovetail marks were not taken from one single template, and the difference shows at the back corner. Cutting makes up part of the ground that was lost, for the shoulders are crisp, the sockets clean, the fit close without ever being forced. Finishing is where the work falls down. Sanding was hurried, grinder marks survive beside the fittings, and wax laid over a surface still carrying dust has set fine scratches into it. What the panel will remember is a sound piece whose last stage gives away the rush of the maker.

units: the maker announces a delay of two weeks on an order
the timber set aside was soaked under a damaged sheet
its moisture is too high for the workshop to accept
using that wood would pull the panels in after assembly
the drawers would bind as soon as the heating went on
the boards have been put into the drying kiln
the work starts again on an older batch
the new colour is darker than expected
photographs will be sent at the dry assembly
text: I am writing about the chest of drawers you left with me, which will now take a fortnight longer than we agreed. The fault lies with the timber. The batch I had set aside spent weeks under a torn sheet, and it has taken up more moisture than my workshop will allow. Were I to use it as it stands, the panels would pull in once assembled and the drawers would bind as soon as the heating went on. So those boards have gone into the drying kiln and I have started cutting again from an older batch, which puts the whole job back. There is one pleasant result: the replacement timber is deeper in tone, and I shall suggest a pale wax to bring that out. I will send you photographs as soon as it stands dry, so that you can settle your choice before a drop of glue is anywhere near it.

units: a furniture restorer is blamed for the slowness of her quotes
every piece hides repairs carried out earlier
an assessment made too fast brings costs nobody planned for
she takes part of the piece apart before naming a price
this inspection is charged to the owner
half of the customers refuse to pay for it
she now offers two ways of quoting
the inspection fee is taken off if the work comes to her
disagreements with customers have almost stopped
text: What does a furniture restorer say when people complain that her quotes take too long? She lays the problem out plainly: every piece hides a history of earlier repairs, and a rushed diagnosis leads to costs nobody planned for. Asked how she works, she describes taking part of the piece apart, testing the glue lines, looking at the backs, and only then naming a price she will stand by. Asked what that care costs, she admits she charges for it and that one owner in two says no. Her answer has been to offer two quotes: a fee for the inspection, taken off the bill if the restoration comes to her, and a broad estimate for anyone who wants a figure on the spot. Since then disagreements have all but vanished. One difficulty stays: persuading an owner in a hurry that patience is cheaper than doing the work twice.
